title: What koans are not
hook: not riddles with clever answers; Soto Zen stresses just sitting instead, and both are Zen

segments.voice: Yesterday: dokusan, and your line, carry it. Today is the last day of the koans.

After two weeks of dogs, bowls, foxes, fingers, flags, flowers, faces, cats, good days and one hand, you might think Zen is basically koans. Step into a Soto Zen hall in Japan and there's something different. People sitting facing a plain wall. No question to hold. No interview bell. Just sitting, for a long time, very still. That's Zen too. Today the koans close with what they aren't, and with the other great way Zen is practiced.
screen: `DOGS, BOWLS, FOXES, FLAGS.` → `PEOPLE FACING A PLAIN WALL.` → `THAT'S ZEN TOO.`

segments.voice: First, what koans are not. They're not riddles with clever answers; the teacher's bell sends clever answers back. They're not nonsense meant to confuse you; each grew out of a real encounter and points somewhere. And they're not the only way to practice Zen. In Japan the two main Zen schools are Rinzai, which you've been meeting, and Soto. Soto was brought from China by a Japanese monk named Dogen. His teacher in China had a phrase for the heart of practice: just sitting. In Japanese, shikantaza. You sit upright, usually facing a wall, eyes half open, and you don't hold a koan, count breaths or aim at anything. You just sit, fully awake to sitting. Remember nothing to attain, from the Heart Sutra: Dogen taught that sitting isn't a means to awakening later. Sitting is awakening, being expressed. The difference isn't new. In Song-dynasty China, Dahui championed working on a single koan phrase, while Hongzhi taught a quiet practice he called silent illumination. They disagreed, and were friends: tradition says Hongzhi asked Dahui to handle his funeral. Today Rinzai teachers stress koans, Soto teachers stress just sitting, and both schools say the other is Zen. Soto teachers study koans too; Dogen wrote about them often. And some lineages, especially in the West, teach both. Two weeks of koans, closed in silence: don't solve it, mu, wash your bowl, not blind to cause, your own finger, mind moves, the smile, before you were born, sandals on the head, every day is a good day, ordinary mind, one hand, carry it. And now, just sitting.
screen: `NOT RIDDLES, NOT NONSENSE.` · `SOTO ZEN AND DOGEN.` · `SHIKANTAZA: JUST SITTING.` · `DAHUI AND HONGZHI, FRIENDS.` · then, large: `JUST SITTING.`

segments.voice: No koan, no counting, no word on the breath: sit upright as if a thread were lifting the crown of your head, eyes resting half open on the floor or a wall a little in front of you. When thoughts come, don't follow them and don't push them away; let them pass like weather. Just this body, sitting, breathing.
Shikantaza. Just sitting, facing a wall, holding no koan and aiming at nothing: the other great way Zen is practiced.
Your line: just sitting. Nothing to solve, nothing to add. That's two weeks of koans, closed.

howItsDone: In Soto Zen, practitioners sit shikantaza, usually facing a wall, without a koan; in Rinzai Zen they usually sit facing into the room and work with koans. Some lineages teach both.

original.note: Japanese shikantaza: 'nothing but sitting', the phrase Dogen took from his teacher Rujing.

trapdoor: what you thought: Zen is basically koans.
what it means: koans are one great way of Zen practice; just sitting is the other, and both are Zen.
what a scholar hears: the twelfth-century debate between Dahui's 'phrase-watching' (kanhua) and Hongzhi's 'silent illumination' (mozhao) shaped the later Rinzai and Soto emphases.

notes: Soto as the largest Zen school in Japan by number of temples: confirm.
Shikantaza as a phrase from Rujing (Tiantong Rujing): confirm.
Hongzhi asking Dahui to oversee his funeral: traditional account; confirm.
Facing the wall (Soto) versus facing the room (Rinzai) is a general custom; varies.
